identity.title: Is God a Figment of Our Imagination? Michael Shermer vs. Alister McGrath (2017)
identity.label: God, imagination, and explanatory evidence
identity.motion: Is God a figment of our imagination?

bridges.statement: The diversity and recurring structure of religious ideas are better explained as human cultural constructions than as perceptions of God.
Claims about God should receive confidence only in proportion to publicly testable evidence, with belief withheld where that evidence is absent.
Competing religions and recurrent myths support a common human storytelling origin rather than the unique truth of one tradition.
Meaning, morality, and social improvement can be grounded in human nature, evidence, and secular institutions without God.
Apparently random suffering and a belief system that credits God only for favorable outcomes undermine claims of divine intervention.
Belief in God is a defensible response to reality and human experience rather than merely a consoling human invention.
Christianity supplies an intellectually and existentially capacious worldview that complements science and illuminates human life.
Ultimate commitments lie beyond demonstrative proof, and changing scientific theories require epistemic modesty from believers and skeptics alike.
Stable meaning, value, and human worth require grounding beyond individual preference or the prejudices of a society.
The Christian account of incarnation and redemptive action makes God relevant within history and motivates resistance to suffering.

moves.speaker: Alister McGrath
moves.excerpt: supposing you and I have been here a hundred years ago when the scientific method was still being used the consensus was the universe had always been here there's been a radical change what was thought then to be true is now known not to be true and if we try and extend ourselves into the future and ask what will people think a hundred years from now we just don't know the answer
moves.proposition: Past cosmological consensus changed radically, so present scientific judgments cannot determine with certainty what future inquiry will conclude.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is McGrath's major direct challenge to Shermer's presentation of science as a settled arbiter.

responseComponents.text: McGrath cautions that what currently appears absent or theoretically required may be reassessed after future scientific change.
He argues that scientific conclusions themselves remain historically revisable, tempering Shermer's sharp evidential asymmetry.

requirements.summaryWords: 22-35 words; state the comparative result and the central reasons without hype
requirements.cardWords: 22-28 words inclusive for every move; convey the locked claim, supporting reason or comparison, and inference, reply target, consequence, or remaining burden
requirements.critique: Exactly four labeled sentences in this order: Strongest feature, Principal limitation, Live burden, Locked score. Target 112-118 words, remain within 105-130 words and at least 880 characters, use exactly one sentence per label, and end each with ordinary terminal punctuation. Every sentence must analyze this move's actual inference, evidence, limitation, burden contact, or score-specific tradeoff. Avoid reusable rubric boilerplate.
requirements.overall: Per side provide exactly four strengths and three blunders. Each item must contain 22-36 words, be move-specific, nonredundant, and consistent with the locked scores. Leave blunder links empty for later independent rhetorical review.
requirements.quotes: Choose one exact, contiguous 3-18-word substring from a supplied move excerpt per side, using different representative moves. Write a 22-38-word source-grounded context for each quote. The quote must match case and punctuation exactly.
requirements.extension: Clearly score-neutral AI steelman. Per side provide a 22-40-word thesis, exactly five 22-40-word premises, a 22-45-word conclusion, and exactly two genuinely reinforcing new arguments of 70-105 words each. Do not attribute AI material to a speaker.
requirements.noveltyMap: Map every thesis, premise, conclusion, and new argument. Use transcript-reinforcement or transcript-repair with related move IDs when grounded in or repairing debate material; use genuinely-new-reinforcement with an empty relatedMoveIds array only when genuinely new.
requirements.punctuation: Use polished ordinary punctuation, including commas where English syntax requires them. Avoid semicolons inside critiques because sentence counting is literal.
requirements.scoreInterpretation: Scores in the 80s indicate strong work with bounded limitations; the 70s are solid but incomplete; the 60s are mixed or under-supported; the 50s are weak. Explain the exact score using its actual dimension pattern, never generic band language alone.
requirements.prohibited: No score changes, invented transcript claims, fallacy or bias tags, outside facts, novelty overclaiming, wording attributed to a speaker outside exact selected quotes, excessive boilerplate, or use of the word unassailable.
